scenes.purpose: Hook: the falling asteroid and what it ended.

visual.title: One very bad day
visual.statement: 66 million years ago, an asteroid strike ended the age of dinosaurs and opened the way for mammals.

narration.text: Sixty-six million years ago, a rock about ten kilometers wide was falling toward Earth at tens of kilometers per second.
Within hours, the world that dinosaurs had dominated for well over a hundred million years began to end.
It was a sudden catastrophe,
followed by years of darkness and cold,
and it cleared the stage for a new world, including, eventually, us.

scenes.purpose: Place the age of dinosaurs in deep time.

narration.text: The first dinosaurs appeared around two hundred thirty million years ago.
After another mass extinction, about two hundred one million years ago, they came to dominate life on land.
Near the end, giants like Tyrannosaurus rex and Triceratops roamed what is now North America.
Then, sixty-six million years ago, it all came crashing down.

scenes.purpose: Give the scale of the extinction and of the asteroid.

visual.title: One of the worst extinctions ever

stats.label: of plant and animal species wiped out

narration.text: It was one of the five worst mass extinctions in Earth's history.
Around three-quarters of all plant and animal species vanished.
And it was triggered by a single asteroid, about ten kilometers across.

scenes.purpose: Contrast the groups that died with those that survived.

narration.text: The losses were uneven.
Every dinosaur that was not a bird died out, along with the flying pterosaurs and the great marine reptiles.
But birds, small mammals, crocodiles and turtles made it through.
Why them? To answer that, scientists first had to work out what happened.

scenes.purpose: Set up the long scientific mystery.

visual.title: A long-running mystery
visual.statement: For more than a century, scientists argued about why the dinosaurs vanished.

narration.text: For more than a century, the cause was a mystery.
Some blamed a slowly changing climate,
others, massive volcanic eruptions in India,
and a daring few suggested something from space.

scenes.purpose: Locate the rock layers at Gubbio.

visual.title: A clue in an Italian gorge

narration.text: The breakthrough came from a gorge near the town of Gubbio, in central Italy.
Its rock layers record millions of years of history, including the moment of the extinction.
Right at that boundary sits a thin layer of clay, about a centimeter thick.

scenes.purpose: Define iridium and why it pointed to space.

visual.title: A metal from space
visual.definition: A metal that is very rare in Earth's crust but far more common in asteroids and meteorites.
visual.example: The boundary clay held dozens of times more iridium than the rock around it.

narration.text: In 1980, physicist Luis Alvarez and his son Walter, a geologist, published their analysis of that clay.
It contained a surprising amount of a metal called iridium.
Iridium is very rare in Earth's crust, but far more common in asteroids.
The clay held dozens of times more of it than the rock around it.

scenes.purpose: Show the reasoning from the iridium spike to the impact theory.

visual.title: From a clue to a theory

narration.text: Then came the key step.
The same iridium spike, right at the boundary,
turned up at sites far apart, from Denmark to New Zealand.
The Alvarez team proposed that an asteroid, roughly ten kilometers wide, had struck the Earth,
spreading its dust around the planet and triggering the extinction.
It was a bold idea, and many scientists doubted it, because nobody could point to a crater.

scenes.purpose: Locate the Chicxulub crater.

narration.text: The crater had been hiding in plain sight.
In 1978, geophysicists searching for oil off Mexico's Yucatan Peninsula found part of a huge buried ring.
By 1991, scientists had shown it was an impact crater of just the right age.
It is named after a nearby village: Chicxulub.

scenes.purpose: Give the size and age of the crater.

narration.text: The crater is about one hundred eighty kilometers across, now buried under younger rock.
Dating of glassy beads from the impact shows it formed sixty-six million years ago, matching the extinction.
The murder weapon had been found.

scenes.purpose: List the other physical evidence of an impact.

visual.title: The fingerprints of an impact
visual.statement: Rocks from that moment, around the Gulf of Mexico and beyond, carry the marks of a giant collision.

narration.text: Other clues backed it up.
Grains of quartz carry shock marks that only extreme impacts can produce.
Tiny glass beads, melted rock flung into the sky, rained down across the Americas.
And jumbled layers around the Gulf of Mexico point to giant tsunamis.

scenes.purpose: Describe what drilling into the crater revealed.

visual.title: Drilling into the crater
visual.statement: In 2016, an expedition drilled more than a kilometer into the crater's buried peak ring.
points: Rock piled up in a single day

narration.text: In 2016, scientists drilled into the crater from a platform off the Yucatan coast.
They pulled up granite from deep underground, shattered and lifted kilometers in a matter of minutes.
Above it lay about one hundred thirty meters of rock that seems to have piled up within a single day.
And the sulfur-rich rocks common in the region were missing, as if the impact had vaporized them.

scenes.purpose: Show the first minutes after the impact.

narration.text: So what happened on that day?
The asteroid struck a shallow sea, releasing billions of times the energy of the Hiroshima bomb.
A fireball and shock wave devastated everything for hundreds of kilometers.
Molten rock was hurled high above the atmosphere,
and tsunamis raced across the Gulf of Mexico and beyond.

scenes.purpose: Lay out how the damage unfolded over time.

narration.text: The damage unfolded on every time scale.
In seconds, a fireball and shock wave tore across the region.
Within hours, falling debris heated the sky, and may have sparked fires far away.
Over the following months, dust, soot and sulfur spread around the globe, blocking sunlight.
And for years afterward, the climate stayed brutally cold.

scenes.purpose: Define impact winter.

visual.title: Darkness at noon
visual.definition: A long stretch of cold and gloom after a huge impact, as dust, soot and sulfur block sunlight.
visual.example: Without light, plants and plankton stopped growing, and food chains collapsed.

narration.text: Scientists call this an impact winter.
Dust, soot and sulfur blocked so much sunlight that the surface plunged into cold and gloom.
Without light, plants and ocean plankton stopped growing, and food chains collapsed from the bottom up.

scenes.purpose: Explain why the location made it worse.

visual.title: The worst possible place
visual.statement: The asteroid hit rocks rich in sulfur, which made the climate disaster far worse.
points: Bad luck in place and timing

narration.text: In some ways, the dinosaurs were unlucky.
The asteroid hit rocks packed with sulfur, which vaporized into sun-blocking droplets.
Computer models suggest it struck at a steep angle, throwing even more gas into the atmosphere.
Some scientists think a strike in most other places, like the deep ocean, would have been far less deadly.

scenes.purpose: Weigh the asteroid against the Deccan volcanoes.

narration.text: One debate remains: what role did the giant volcanoes of India play?
The asteroid explains the sudden, worldwide collapse, and the timing fits precisely.
But the Deccan eruptions released vast amounts of gas over hundreds of thousands of years, and may have stressed life beforehand.
Most scientists now see the asteroid as the decisive blow.

scenes.purpose: Explain why some animals survived.

visual.title: How to survive the end of the world
visual.statement: The survivors tended to be small, sheltered and able to eat whatever was left.

narration.text: So why did some animals make it?
Small animals needed less food and bred quickly.
Burrowers and freshwater creatures were sheltered from the worst of the heat and cold.
And animals that ate seeds, insects or decaying matter could live off the ruins of the old food web.

scenes.purpose: Explain that birds are surviving dinosaurs.

visual.title: The dinosaurs are still here
visual.definition: Birds: the one branch of the dinosaur family tree that survived the extinction.
visual.example: A sparrow is a closer relative of T. rex than a crocodile is.

narration.text: In fact, the dinosaurs did not entirely disappear.
Biologists call birds avian dinosaurs.
They are the one branch of the dinosaur family tree that survived the extinction.
A sparrow is a closer relative of Tyrannosaurus rex than a crocodile is.

scenes.purpose: Show how life recovered and mammals rose.

narration.text: Remarkably, life returned to the crater itself within just a few years.
Within a million years, mammals were growing larger and more varied.
Over the next ten million years, mammals spread into roles the dinosaurs had left empty, including early primates.
Today, mammals, including us, are the largest animals on land.

scenes.purpose: Put the risk of another impact in perspective.

stats.label: years between impacts this large, roughly
of near-Earth asteroids over 1 km already found

narration.text: Could it happen again?
Impacts this size are rare, roughly once every hundred million years.
Astronomers have found over ninety percent of near-Earth asteroids a kilometer or larger, and none is on a collision course.

scenes.purpose: Explain planetary defense.

narration.text: And unlike the dinosaurs, we can look up and plan.
Telescopes scan the sky for asteroids,
and astronomers track their orbits decades into the future.
In 2022, NASA's DART spacecraft crashed into a small asteroid and changed its orbit, proving deflection can work.
With enough warning, a dangerous rock could be nudged off course.

scenes.purpose: Close with what the impact means for us.

visual.title: A world shaped by chance
visual.statement: Without that asteroid, mammals might never have risen, and humans might never have existed.

narration.text: Sixty-six million years ago, a random rock from space rewrote the history of life.
It ended the age of dinosaurs, and opened the age of mammals.
In a sense, every one of us is here because of the worst day the dinosaurs ever had.
So the next time a bird lands near your window, remember: you are looking at a survivor of that day.
